transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I know this is a packed week. I'm Ethan from Redwood, with Priya - our solutions engineer - and Samir from product success. Today we'll walk through structured output/JSON mode and the function calling/tooling in the Console and via API.
[00:18] Lucas Nguyen: Great, thanks. We're excited — our main use case is generating transaction interpretation JSONs for downstream rules engines, so schema enforcement and reliability are big for us.
[00:30] Priya Rao: Perfect. We'll start with a short API demo then hop into the Console for schema setup and Optimize suggests. Quick question — do you have an existing schema style, like JSON Schema or a custom model?
[00:42] Tara Singh: We use a mix — some teams publish json-schema, others have internal protobufs. Ideally Redwood can validate and also return structured objects we can ingest.
[00:55] Priya Rao: Yes, JSON mode supports schema validation and we can map to your protobufs in the pipeline. We'll show a live example.
[01:05] Ethan Carter: A couple of things to flag: we'll also demo guardrails — like strict vs permissive mode — and how the system falls back to a compatible model variant if the primary model is overloaded.
[01:18] Rory Blake: On the fallback, is that per-route? We can't have sensitive data leave our VPC if it's on-prem.
[01:24] Samir Joshi: Good callout. For Private deployments you keep the control plane in your VPC; fallbacks are configurable — we can restrict cross-region/model fallbacks for regulated workloads.
[01:35] Lucas Nguyen: Ok cool.
[01:38] [Demo start - API]
[01:40] Priya Rao: I'm running a short generation where we ask the model to parse a transaction note and return an object with fields: merchant_name, amount, currency, category, suspicious_flag. In JSON mode we pass a schema and a strict flag. I'll paste the request: POST /v1/generate with mode=json, schema=orderSchema_v2.
[02:05] Priya Rao: (typing) ... response coming in — you'll see streaming tokens but the SDK assembles structured result.
[02:18] [02:18] Priya Rao: And here's the output: {"merchant_name":"Acme Supply","amount":124.53,"currency":"USD","category":"Office","suspicious_flag":false} — note that the output validated against the schema.
[02:35] Lucas Nguyen: I see. What happens if the model hallucinate a field?
[02:40] Priya Rao: In strict mode the SDK rejects outputs that don't match schema and returns a validation error, we also provide partial outputs with diagnostics. In permissive mode it tries to coerce or return best-effort with warnings.
[02:52] Tara Singh: Is that validation client-side or server-side?
[02:55] Priya Rao: Server-side at the Redwood runtime — reduces client complexity and ensures consistent enforcement across routes.
[03:03] [03:03] Lucas Nguyen: What's the performance impact? We care about p95 latency.
[03:08] Priya Rao: Small overhead for validation — usually <20ms post-tokenization for medium schemas. Biggest latency levers are model size and KV cache hit rate. Which p95 are you aiming for?
[03:20] Lucas Nguyen: Under 300ms for simple parsers, 500ms maybe acceptable for complex ones.
[03:26] Priya Rao: We showed Optimize earlier on a similar workload and recommended a quantized 8-bit variant with prefix caching; that dropped token cost by ~40% while keeping p95 under 280ms in our benchmark. We'll share the spreadsheet.
[03:40] [03:40] Ethan Carter: Now switching to function/tool calling — this is helpful when you want the model to produce structured calls to internal tools or downstream microservices. Priya, can you demo the function call to our validation service?
[03:52] Priya Rao: Yep. I'm toggling function_call: enabled and passing a schema that maps to an internal endpoint validateTransaction(). In the Console we can register functions and expected JSON signatures.
[04:06] Priya Rao: (demo) The model returns a function call: {"name":"validateTransaction","arguments":{"merchant_name":"Acme Supply","amount":124.53}}. Redwood then executes the function (we've hooked a mock endpoint) and attaches the result back into the conversation.
[04:23] Lucas Nguyen: So Redwood actually invokes our function? How do we secure that?
[04:28] Samir Joshi: The runtime only calls endpoints you register. For Private/VPC deployments the calls happen over your private network. We also support signing and mutual TLS, and KMS-backed secrets for webhook credentials.
[04:39] Tara Singh: Sounds promising. Any misfires — like the model calling wrong endpoint — how do you guard?
[04:44] Priya Rao: You can pin permissible function names per-route, whitelist schemas, and the Console warns on unknown signatures. Plus we keep a trace and audit log for every function invocation.
[04:56] [05:00] Lucas Nguyen: Audit logs — is that SOC 2 level? We need retention for audits.
[05:04] Ethan Carter: We provide configurable retention, export to your SIEM, and can integrate with cloud KMS or customer-managed HSMs for keying. SOC 2 and ISO are available — we'll share the security packet.
[05:18] [Console walkthrough]
[05:20] Priya Rao: Now in Console — here's a route: /transactions/parse. You can add a schema (we support JSON Schema draft-07 style), set strict/permissive, attach model policies, and add Optimize suggestions. You can also upload sample prompts for regression tests.
[05:38] Priya Rao: Watch the guardrail toggle — when strict is on, you'll see pre-deployment checks flag if sample prompts produce schema violations. You can set auto-block or auto-log.
[05:50] Tara Singh: If we enable auto-block, will we risk increased error rates affecting SLAs?
[05:56] Priya Rao: It depends — blocking will increase apparent errors but prevents bad downstream data. Many teams do blocking in staging and permissive in prod with alerts. Optimize can suggest thresholds based on observed false-positive rates.
[06:12] Lucas Nguyen: Can Optimize recommend batching sizes? Our throughput is variable — payroll end-of-month is huge.
[06:18] Priya Rao: Yes — Optimize analyzes request patterns, suggests batching and cache TTLs; for bursty loads we recommend reserved Dedicated pools with burst capacity to keep p95 stable.
[06:30] Rory Blake: Dedicated raises cost — how deterministic are your recommendations?
[06:34] Ethan Carter: We surface expected unit economics and show historical cluster utilization models. It's a recommendation — final decision depends on your SLA and budget. We can run a short pilot to measure.
[06:46] [06:46] Lucas Nguyen: On data residency: we need EU tenant isolation for some customers. Can you pin models and runtime region?
[06:52] Samir Joshi: Yes, you can pin region and model variants; in Private deployment you control the region. For Hosted we offer region restrictions and data residency controls.
[07:02] [Interruption — connection glitch, 7 seconds of audio drop] 
[07:10] Priya Rao: Back — sorry, small glitch. Moving on to error handling patterns. We'll show sample diagnostic logs in the Console.
[07:18] Priya Rao: Here is a run where the model produced an unexpected "merchant" object. Console highlights the schema violation and shows token-level trace so you can see where the divergence occurred.
[07:30] Lucas Nguyen: The token trace — is that available for all customers? PII concerns.
[07:35] Ethan Carter: It's configurable — you can mask or redact by default, and redact PII before it's stored in logs. We also support token-level hashing for analytics without storing raw text.
[07:47] Tara Singh: How do we integrate with our SSO?
[07:50] Priya Rao: SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported; RBAC maps to routes and team scopes. We'll send the integration guide.
[07:58] [08:00] Lucas Nguyen: A few nitty-gritty: 1) Does schema validation block token generation or post-validate? 2) Can we have schema versioning and rollbacks? 3) How to test with canaries?
[08:12] Priya Rao: 1) It's post-validate on generation but we can run pre-deploy sample test to catch obvious issues. 2) Console supports schema versioning; you can pin routes to specific schema versions. 3) Canary rollouts are first-class: route-level canary, A/B, and automatic fallback on error budget.
[08:29] Lucas Nguyen: Good.
[08:31] [08:31] Priya Rao: I'll show function-calling with an attached transform step — model returns the function call, we run an internal transform, and then the final JSON is canonicalized. You can view each step in the trace.
[08:46] Lucas Nguyen: For the transform step do you allow customer code? We run proprietary classification for some categories.
[08:51] Samir Joshi: Yes, you can host transforms as customer-managed lambdas in your VPC and Redwood will call them via private link. We maintain an execution trace but not the code.
[08:59] [09:00] Tara Singh: Any failover if the transform lambda times out?
[09:03] Priya Rao: We have configurable retry and fallback policies — you can route to a secondary transform or return a partial response with a flag.
[09:12] [09:12] Lucas Nguyen: About costs — tool calling adds extra compute; do you bill function invocations separately?
[09:18] Ethan Carter: We bill per-token generation and for optional execution blocks (like calling managed tools) there's a small per-call fee for hosted tool execution. For Private you can control whether to execute tools via Redwood or entirely within your infra.
[09:30] [09:30] Lucas Nguyen: Is there sample code for SDK integration?
[09:33] Priya Rao: Yes, GitHub repo link pasted in chat: https://redwood.ai/sdks/structured-output-demo (note: link in transcript for reference).
[09:42] [Questions from Maya Ortiz — Product]
[09:44] Maya Ortiz: If we want to expose an audit trail to end users (e.g., in a dispute flow), can we surface the model decision path?
[09:50] Priya Rao: You can expose a curated trace that shows schema hits, function calls, and non-sensitive token highlights. We advise redaction for PII.
[09:59] Rory Blake: Ok, I'm thinking about the pilot — we'd want a 4-week POC: ingest sample data, run 10k requests/day and measure p95, failure modes, and cost. Can Redwood help instrument that?
[10:10] Ethan Carter: Absolutely. Typical pilot includes a reserved trial cluster for predictable metrics, shared dashboard access, and weekly syncs. We'll propose scope in the SOW.
[10:20] Lucas Nguyen: Perfect.
[10:22] [Wrap-up and Recap]
[10:23] Ethan Carter: Quick recap — we demoed JSON mode with strict vs permissive validation, function calling with registered endpoints, console guardrails and pre-deploy checks, Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization, and Private/VPC options for security. Agreed next steps: we'll send pricing/pilot SOW, Priya will share benchmark spreadsheet/runbook, customer to share prompts/schemas, and we'll schedule an infra deep-dive.
[10:45] Tara Singh: Thanks, Ethan, Priya. We'll get the artifacts over this week.
[10:50] Ethan Carter: Thanks everyone.
[10:52] [Call end]
